<reason>CON (A) built the stronger path on a conjunctive motion. Its decisive move was neutralizing PRO's core mechanism: PRO argued a nationwide mandate closes the escape valve, but CON showed Arizona's mandate produced off-payroll displacement within the same county, leaving PRO with only a burden-shifting "absorption capacity unproven" reply against the one real-world observation. On shortages, CON conceded B's H-2A catch (no statutory cap) but pivoted effectively to de facto constraints, using B's own concession that "processing and logistics remain constraints," and showed the new-hire/turnover argument fails where crews are rehired wholesale each season. On discrimination, CON's mechanism (mismatch costs attach only to foreign-seeming applicants) and the invisible-victim point were answered only by after-the-fact statistical detection, which CON fairly rebranded as measuring harm rather than preventing it. PRO was disciplined and honest, and its closing asymmetry critique was its best move, but CON's downhill/uphill reframe answered it directly. PRO's refusal to quantify the residual reduction, against CON's anchored "half clear the check" evidence, left the motion's first prong thin. Both sides avoided fake precision; CON simply landed more damaging reframes of PRO's own answers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1/2 sequence on efficacy: Arizona workers shifted off-payroll in the same county, so nationwide coverage closes the wrong border—PRO never regained that ground, retreating to an unquantified "material decline."</best_rebuttal>
